Vulnerabilities.Title: git: git: Heap corruption via integer overflow in merge size calculations
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Affected versions of Git have a heap buffer overflow in the three-way merge
code (xdiff), which an attacker can trigger through a repository they
control.

When Git merges a file, it first adds up the size of the merged
output, allocates a buffer of that size, and then writes the output into
it. That total was kept in a 32-bit signed integer. The
conflict-marker-size attribute, which can be set from a committed
.gitattributes file, accepts any positive integer, and the markers are
written several times for every conflict. A small file with a huge marker
size and many separate conflicts can therefore push the total past 4 GiB,
so the integer wraps to a small value and Git writes attacker-controlled
merge output past the end of a buffer that is too small. At minimum this
crashes Git, and because the overflow is large and its contents are largely
attacker-controlled, worse heap corruption is possible.

Any command that does a textual three-way merge can trigger it, such
as git-merge(1), git-rebase(1), git-cherry-pick(1), and
git-merge-tree(1). The latter is most likely a target for Git forges,
which might use git-merge-tree(1) on the server-side to check
mergeability. When the server reads attributes from trees in the
repository (for example through attr.tree or --attr-source), any
user who can push branches and request that they be merged (for
example by opening a pull or merge request) can trigger the overflow
without anyone else doing anything, and the data they push is small
because the oversized output only appears during the merge.

The problem has been patched by computing the size as size_t and
checking every addition for overflow, so Git stops with an error
instead of overflowing.

Servers that cannot upgrade right away can add

* conflict-marker-size=7

to each repository's info/attributes as a workaround, which overrides
any in-tree .gitattributes, or turn off server-side mergeability checks for
untrusted repositories.

Vulnerabilities.Title: git: Git: Arbitrary code execution via unsafe submodule metadata during recursive clones
Vulnerabilities.Description: Git is a fast, scalable, distributed revision control system with an unusually rich command set that provides both high-level operations and full access to internals. Prior to 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1, 2.55.1, and 2.56.1, an attacker-controlled repository hosted by the attacker rather than on a normal forge site can exploit git clone --recurse-submodules by causing Git to overwrite a submodule gitfile with a symbolic link. The symbolic link can point to a directory containing attacker-controlled Git configuration or hooks, allowing those hooks or configuration to execute code on the cloning user's system. The issue requires the recursive-submodule option, and users should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources. This issue is fixed in versions 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1, 2.55.1, and 2.56.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via crafted EC certificate in CMS encryption
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order
is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.

Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an
application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop
indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or
more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral
key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1,
random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine
then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the
call never returns.

The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application
is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient
certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with
normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.

OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds.
These versions are affected only when configured with the
enable-ec_explicit_curves option.

The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is
interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker
must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to
encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.

The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero
private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider
does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group
is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is
reached.

Vulnerabilities.Title: openssl: openssl: Denial of Service via overlapping QUIC CRYPTO frame processing
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Issue summary: A retransmitted QUIC CRYPTO frame can release packet storage
while the TLS record layer retains a direct pointer into that storage causing
use after free.

Impact summary: A malicious QUIC server can cause a heap-use-after-free read
in the OpenSSL QUIC client. The server can also identify one allocator-adjacent
byte through the client's protected Handshake response.

CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free

Description: During CRYPTO stream processing, a pointer into the first frame's
memory on the stream is lent to the TLS handshake processing. The memory
must remain stable until it is processed and released. However the processing
of retransmitted CRYPTO frames could release the memory if the retransmitted
frame fully overlapped the existing frame. This then causes use-after-free read
when the TLS handshake processing continues.

The use-after-free read can lead to a Denial-of-Service of the client
application or a minor leak of information about the heap memory contents
that might be overwritten with other data, subsequently allocated by
the application, to the peer.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside of
the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

Vulnerabilities.Title: openssl: OpenSSL: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in AES-GCM-SIV
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Issue summary: Setting an AES-GCM-SIV IV shorter than the expected nonce
length via EVP_CipherInit_ex() may trigger a heap out-of-bounds read.
Supplying a longer IV is silently truncated instead of rejected.

Impact summary: An application passing a caller-supplied IV of the wrong
length may crash or read beyond its buffer. Because trailing IV bytes are
ignored, an attacker who knows one message and tag may forge messages under a
different IV.

CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read

Description: AES-GCM-SIV copies the caller-supplied IV or nonce into its
internal state using a copy whose length is taken from the expected nonce size
rather than from the length the caller actually provided. When the caller
passes a shorter IV, the copy reads past the end of the caller's buffer;
AddressSanitizer confirms a heap out-of-bounds read reached through
EVP_CipherInit_ex() into ossl_aes_gcm_siv_init(). When the caller passes a
longer IV, the implementation silently discards the trailing bytes instead of
rejecting the length.

The truncation breaks the binding between the IV and the computed
authentication tag. An attacker who has observed a message and its tag under
one IV can produce a message and tag that verify under a different IV whose
first bytes match, since the surplus bytes never influence the computation.
The message itself is unchanged, so this is a failure of IV commitment rather
than a classic existential forgery.

Only applications that call EVP_CipherInit_ex() (or the equivalent provider
cipher initialization) with an IV length other than the standard 12 bytes for
AES-GCM-SIV are affected. The severity is limited because the out-of-bounds
read is small and attacker-controlled only in length, and the forgery requires
an unusual IV length choice by the application.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules are not affected by this issue, as AES-GCM-SIV is not an
approved algorithm.

Vulnerabilities.Title: openssl: openssl: Information disclosure via uninitialized memory in QUIC peer detection
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Issue summary: QUIC, when performing automated peer detection, may allow
uninitialized stack data to leak into the received address which is then used
as the destination for outgoing packets.

Impact summary: Applications using QUIC's automated peer detection mechanism
may receive an invalid address, leading to connection loss and disclosure of
uninitialized stack data to an attacker observing the outgoing network traffic.

CWE: CWE-457 (Use of Uninitialized Variable)

Description: The OpenSSL QUIC stack contains a feature in which, when using an
already connected socket, it will auto-detect the peer address during the SSL
handshake.  This feature uses the getpeername() function, passing a buffer of
sufficient length to hold any supported address family, but passes a buffer
length that is only sized such that larger addresses, such as IPv6, cannot be
retrieved. The getpeername() function however, still returns the full address
length, which is accepted as the valid input buffer length, leading to the
address buffer containing uninitialized stack data instead of the actual peer
address. The invalid peer address is then used as destination for the outgoing
packets which leads to a connectivity breakage and a leakage of the
uninitialized stack data to passive network observers.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules in 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, and 3.0 are not affected by this CVE as
the affected protocol is not implemented in the FIPS module.

Vulnerabilities.Title: openssl: OpenSSL: Message authentication bypass via zero-length AAD update
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Issue summary: The AES-GCM-SIV implementation treats a zero-length Additional
Authenticated Data (AAD) update as a reset of all the AAD supplied so far,
instead of leaving the AAD unchanged. An application that supplies its AAD in
several fragments, one of which is empty, therefore produces or verifies
messages whose authentication tag does not cover the AAD supplied before
the empty fragment.

Impact summary: Data an application intended to authenticate alongside a
message is silently left unauthenticated. An attacker can forge the AAD of such
a message.

CWE: CWE-325: Missing Cryptographic Step

Description: An application passing AAD in multiple chunks of which some have
zero length will have the previous AAD chunks effectively unauthenticated. Also,
on context re-initialisation, the AAD was not reset, which meant that any AAD
accumulated from the previous context usage were also included in the AAD of the
new message.

The fix makes a zero-length AAD update a no-op and clears any accumulated AAD
whenever the context is re-initialised with a key or a nonce.
A re-initialisation that only changes parameters keeps the AAD.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules are not affected, as AES-GCM-SIV is not a FIPS approved
algorithm and is implemented only in the default provider, outside the
OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

Vulnerabilities.Title: libexpat through 2.10.0 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability i ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: libexpat through 2.10.0 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in unknown_toUtf8() and unknown_toUtf16() in xmltok.c when handling application-registered unknown encodings. Attackers can supply a document ending in a truncated multibyte sequence so the convert callback reads past the parse buffer, leaking adjacent memory or crashing applications.

Vulnerabilities.Title: The xmlwf tool in libexpat through 2.10.0 contains a symlink following ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: The xmlwf tool in libexpat through 2.10.0 contains a symlink following vulnerability because -d output mode opens files with fopen("wb"), which follows symbolic links. Local attackers with write access to the output directory can plant a symlink at the expected output name to truncate or overwrite files writable by the xmlwf user.

Vulnerabilities.Title: libexpat through 2.10.0 contains an improper Unicode handling vulnerab ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: libexpat through 2.10.0 contains an improper Unicode handling vulnerability in DEFINE_UTF16_TO_UTF16 conversion functions in xmltok.c that can split valid surrogate pairs when output space is limited. In XML_UNICODE builds parsing non-native byte order UTF-16 input, attackers can supply crafted documents that deliver lone high surrogates to character data and default handlers.

Vulnerabilities.Title: addressable: addressable: Hostname spoofing via invalid Punycode decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, the pure-Ruby Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode implementation decodes invalid Punycode A-labels instead of returning them unchanged. Labels that decode to ASCII text or fail to convert back to the same A-label can therefore make Addressable::URI#display_uri show a trusted-looking host while host, normalized_host, and the connection target retain the attacker-controlled encoded host. A trusted-name comparison using Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode output can also treat two different hosts as the same without displaying the URI. The native libidn implementation, to_ascii, and normalized_host are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.3.0 until 2.9.1, URI template expressions using the explode modifier with the slash, dot, semicolon, question-mark, or ampersand operators generate ambiguous regular expressions. When Template#match or Template#extract processes an attacker-controlled URI beginning with the operator's leading character, optional member separators allow catastrophic backtracking and denial of service on MRI Ruby before 3.2 and JRuby. Addressable 2.9.0 incompletely remediated the earlier template issue because its tests did not reach these operator-prefixed paths. URI parsing and Template#expand are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. Prior to 2.9.1, Addressable::URI.normalize_path repeatedly scans and rewrites paths while removing only one nested dot segment per pass, producing quadratic work. URI#normalize, URI#normalized_path, URI#join, URI#==, and URI#=== inherit the behavior, so processing a sufficiently long attacker-controlled URI can consume a worker thread and cause denial of service on every Ruby implementation. URI.parse alone and code that never normalizes, compares, or joins untrusted URIs are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: addressable: addressable: Denial of Service via regular expression backtracking in URI templates
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.3.0 until 2.9.1, URI templates with several variables in one expression or several adjacent expressions generate ambiguous regular expressions. Affected forms include multi-variable expressions using operators other than plus and number sign, large plus or number-sign expressions, and adjacent single-variable expressions. Template#match or Template#extract can backtrack polynomially or exponentially on attacker-controlled URIs, causing denial of service on MRI Ruby before 3.2 and JRuby, with the large plus and number-sign form also affecting MRI Ruby 3.2 and TruffleRuby 40.0. URI parsing and Template#expand are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation ...
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.2.5 until 2.9.1, Addressable::URI.normalize_path can resolve a path containing leading parent segments and later parent segments to a different path than an RFC 3986 resolver. URI#normalize, URI#join, URI#==, and URI#=== inherit the result. An application that authorizes the Addressable-normalized path but sends the original URI to another resolver can allow access outside the intended path allowlist. Applications that use the same normalized value for authorization and the request, or reject parent segments, are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with several exploded variables
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, expressions
with several exploded variables (e.g., {+a*,b*}, {+a*,b*,c*},
{/a*,b*}, {?a*,b*}) generate regular expressions vulnerable to
excessive backtracking. A run of members can be divided among the
exploded variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables. When Template#match
or Template#extract is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this
can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial
of service. With 2.9.0, {+a*,b*,c*} takes over 12 seconds to reject
1 KB of input on MRI Ruby 3.2.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only
call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported by Daniel Coles (@manus-pi).

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::URI.normalize_path resolves some paths containing ..
segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs
above the root before any other .. is resolved, the segments that
later .. segments should remove are instead kept:
/../../public/x/../../secret normalizes to /public/x/secret instead
of /secret. URI#normalize, URI#join, URI#== and URI#=== all use
this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable
path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something
that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a
request for a path outside the allowlist.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation,
decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with xn--) that are not
valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when
they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

* labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. xn--google-
  decodes to google;
* labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same
  label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so for
https://xn--google-.example.org/ it displays the host google.example.org,
while #host, #normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
use xn--google-.example.org. An attacker who controls a domain can
therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control.
Applications that compare the result of to_unicode against a list
of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, is not affected. to_ascii and normalized_host
are not affected.

## Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

Vulnerabilities.Title: addressable: addressable: Hostname spoofing via improper Unicode character decoding
Vulnerabilities.Description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode can decode Punycode labels that contain bidirectional controls, zero-width characters, control characters, or other default-ignorable format characters. Addressable::URI#display_uri can consequently show a reordered or visually indistinguishable hostname even though host, normalized_host, and network connections use the original encoded hostname. The pure-Ruby backend accepts the full prohibited set, while the native libidn backend is affected from 2.5.2 for characters added after Unicode 3.2. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning
with xn--) that contain characters which change how text is displayed
without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls
such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width
characters, and other invisible format characters.
Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so it can display a
host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to
a different host. For example, the host of http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/
is displayed as abc, U+202E, moc.com, and the override makes
everything after abc render right to left.

Parsing, host, normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that
show display_uri to users (link previews, chat and email clients,
admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look
like a trusted one.

In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are
decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters
added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

## Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

Vulnerabilities.Title: json: Ruby JSON: Denial of Service via heap-use-after-free in JSON::ResumableParser
Vulnerabilities.Description: Ruby JSON is a JSON implementation for Ruby. From 2.20.0 until 2.21.2, Ruby's JSON native C extension clears the consumed JSON::ResumableParser input buffer but leaves state.start, state.cursor, and state.end pointing into released storage. When partial_value reconstructs an incomplete object containing duplicate keys, the duplicate-key warning path calls cursor_position, which dereferences those stale pointers. This results in a heap-use-after-free and can terminate the Ruby process. An attacker who can supply JSON stream data to an application using JSON::ResumableParser may cause process termination when the application calls partial_value on incomplete attacker-controlled input containing duplicate object keys. This issue has been fixed in version 2.21.2.

Vulnerabilities.Title: json: Ruby JSON: Denial of service via heap buffer overflow with oversized streamed objects
Vulnerabilities.Description:
Ruby JSON is a JSON implementation for Ruby. Versions 2.9.0 through 2.19.8 are vulnerable to heap buffer overflow when the JSON generator is provided with an oversized streamed object. When streaming to an IO JSON.dump(obj, io) and JSON::State#generate(obj, io) can write past the internal JSON generator buffer when a streamed object contains an
attacker-controlled string near 16 KB. Exploitation would result in a reliable process crash/denial of service. This issue has been fixed in version 2.19.9.

Vulnerabilities.Title: nokogiri: nokogiri: Server-Side Request Forgery via network restriction bypass on JRuby
Vulnerabilities.Description: Nokogiri is an open source XML and HTML library for the Ruby programming language. Prior to 1.19.5, on JRuby, applications that parse untrusted XML with DTDLOAD, DTDVALID, or NOENT can have the NONET restriction bypassed when an external DTD or entity uses a short-form IPv4 host or uses absolute paths resolved against a network URL. The resolver can treat these identifiers as local and send a network request, potentially enabling server-side request forgery. CRuby and default parse options are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.19.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: nokogiri: nokogiri: Cross-site scripting via unescaped content in HTML5 serializer
Vulnerabilities.Description: Nokogiri is an open source XML and HTML library for the Ruby programming language. From 1.12.0 until 1.19.5, the C extension on CRuby and TruffleRuby has a Nokogiri::HTML5 serializer that does not escape text inside noscript elements or angle brackets inside attribute values. When an application sanitizes untrusted HTML with the default parsing options, allows noscript, and sends serialized output to a scripting-enabled browser, the browser can parse markup that Nokogiri did not produce, enabling mutation cross-site scripting. Using parse_noscript_content_as_text: true is the recommended workaround, not the vulnerable default. JRuby is not affected because it does not implement Nokogiri::HTML5. This issue is fixed in version 1.19.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: nokogiri: nokogiri: Denial of Service via use-after-free when replacing attribute values
Vulnerabilities.Description: Nokogiri is an open source XML and HTML library for the Ruby programming language. Prior to 1.19.5, the CRuby native extension can leave Ruby wrappers pointing to freed memory when Nokogiri::XML::Node#[]= or Nokogiri::XML::Node#lang= replaces an existing attribute value after code has accessed the attribute's child nodes. Replacing the value frees native child nodes while their wrappers remain reachable, and later use of those wrappers can cause an invalid read or process segfault. JRuby is not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.19.5.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Possible SSRF on JRuby when resolving external DTDs or entities with `NONET` set
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

On JRuby, the `NONET` parse option did not block an external DTD or entity
whose system identifier used a short-form IPv4 host, such as `http://127.1/`
or `http://169.254.43518/`, or was an absolute path such as `/x.dtd` in a
document parsed from a network URL. An application that parses untrusted XML
with `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or `NOENT` could be made to send network requests,
potentially enabling SSRF.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 applies the `XML::Schema` check from
[GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-8678-w3jw-xfc2):
with `NONET` set, only local resources are loaded.

Only JRuby is affected. Default parse options are not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity (CVSS 3.7).

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later, or do not enable `DTDLOAD`, `DTDVALID` or
`NOENT` for untrusted input.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @arpitjain099.

Vulnerabilities.Title: Use-After-Free in Nokogiri when replacing an attribute value
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's CRuby native extension could leave a Ruby wrapper pointing to freed
memory when replacing the value of an existing XML attribute via
`Nokogiri::XML::Node#[]=` or `Nokogiri::XML::Node#lang=`. If Ruby code had
already accessed the attribute's child nodes, replacing the value could free
those native child nodes while their wrappers remained reachable. Using one of
those child nodes afterwards could cause an invalid read and a possible
segfault.

This is the same class of issue as
[GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp),
which was fixed for `Attr#value=` in Nokogiri 1.19.4.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 preserves all already-wrapped attribute child nodes before
replacing the attribute value.

JRuby is not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity. Reaching it
requires an unusual API-usage pattern that does not arise during normal use.
The application must directly access an attribute's child nodes and then
replace that same attribute's value via `Node#[]=` or `Node#lang=`. Nokogiri
1.19.5 makes this pattern safe with no change to the public API.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

As a workaround, avoid accessing attribute child nodes directly via
`Attr#children` or similar before replacing the same attribute's value.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by zx (@manus-pi).

Vulnerabilities.Title: Possible Mutation XSS when serializing `noscript` content in `Nokogiri::HTML5` documents
Vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's HTML5 serializer did not escape text inside `noscript` elements, or
`<` and `>` inside attribute values. When a document parsed with the default
options is serialized, a browser with scripting enabled can parse the output
into markup that Nokogiri's parser never produced. This is a mutation XSS for
applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with `Nokogiri::HTML5`, allow
`noscript` elements, and send the serialized output to browsers.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes both, as the HTML standard's serialization algorithm
requires. Text inside `noscript` is still emitted unescaped for documents
parsed with `parse_noscript_content_as_text: true`.

Only the C extension (CRuby and TruffleRuby) is affected. JRuby does not
implement `Nokogiri::HTML5`.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity (CVSS 2.3,
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`).
Exploitation requires an application that allows `noscript` in sanitized HTML.
Loofah and rails-html-sanitizer do not allow it by default, and Sanitize
always removes it.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

Applications that sanitize HTML and allow `noscript` should parse with
`parse_noscript_content_as_text: true` (available since Nokogiri 1.17.0), or
remove `noscript` elements. This is the workaround for earlier versions, and
it is recommended on every version: some content inside `noscript` is
serialized unchanged, as the standard requires.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @a-zara-n.
